content: Ocular injuries are a preventable cause of blindness, yet they continue to represent a significant public health issue that affects individuals across all age groups. These injuries can occur in various settings, including the home, workplace, recreational environments, or as a result of road traffic accidents. The types of ocular injuries range from closed globe injuries, such as contusions or lamellar lacerations, to open globe injuries, which may involve penetration or even perforation of the globe. The primary strategy for preventing these injuries has been to educate individuals to recognize high-risk situations and take appropriate actions to mitigate potential dangers. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the effectiveness of educational interventions in preventing eye injuries. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries and Cochrane Eyes & Vision Group Specialised Registers, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others. The search also included grey literature sources, such as unpublished and ongoing trials, and was last updated in August 2008. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled before-and-after studies that assessed any educational intervention aimed at preventing eye injuries. Four authors independently screened the search results and extracted data, while three authors entered the data into RevMan 5. Due to significant heterogeneity in the participants and interventions across the studies, the results were not pooled but were instead reviewed narratively. The review included two RCTs and three controlled before-and-after studies. Among these, only one study reported eye injuries as an outcome, while the remaining four studies focused on changes in behavior or knowledge. The authors concluded that the included studies do not provide reliable evidence to support the effectiveness of educational interventions in preventing eye injuries. They emphasized the need for well-designed RCTs with proper allocation concealment and blinding. Additionally, future studies should include longer follow-up periods and focus on populations in lowand middle-income countries, where the burden of ocular injuries may be particularly significant.
